extra.message: Authorization bypass via assign_reviewer — underwriter can self-assign to any application — Underwriter can view draft application PII and financial data, steal applications from other underwriters by overwriting assigned_underwriter_id, and subsequently approve or reject stolen applications [verified: The assign_reviewer endpoint at line ~366 loads an application via _load_app() and permits self-assignment with only a role gate (admin/underwriter) — no can_view_application() visibility check, unlike every other application endpoint (get, transition, notes, messages, decisions, documents). An underwriter can POST /applications/{draft_app_id}/assign with their own underwriter_id to gain access to]

Hardcoded database credentials in default configuration — If the default database URL is used and the PostgreSQL instance is network-accessible, an attacker could gain direct database access with full read/write to all PII, financial data, password hashes, and audit logs. [verified: Default database_url contains hardcoded credentials lending_user:lending_pass; no startup guard prevents production deployment with these defaults. The postgresql host is localhost which limits remote exploitation to attackers with local server access, reducing severity from the claimed critical.]

Missing authorization on add_note — underwriters can write internal notes to any application without assignment or visibility check — Underwriter can add internal notes to draft and withdrawn applications they are not assigned to, bypassing the view/assignment controls enforced on other endpoints, enabling unauthorized data access and modification. [verified: add_note only calls can_write_internal_notes(actor) which checks role but omits can_view_application — the latter gates underwriters from draft/withdrawn apps they are not assigned to, and every other endpoint (list_notes, get_application, transition, post_message) enforces it; an unassigned underwriter can write internal notes to draft/withdrawn applications they should have no access to.]

Session cookie missing Secure flag — transmitted over unencrypted HTTP — Network attackers on the same LAN or compromised WiFi can intercept session cookies via passive sniffing and hijack user sessions. [verified: _set_session_cookie at auth.py line 54 hardcodes secure=False with no configuration toggle or proxy-aware header check; the cookie can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, enabling network-level session hijacking despite HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax mitigations.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints enables brute force and abuse — Attackers can brute-force login credentials within the lockout window (8 attempts per 15 min per account), flood the system with fake registrations, and abuse the password-reset flow to spam users. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware or dependency exists anywhere in the codebase; login has per-account lockout (8 failures/15 min) but registration and password-reset have zero throttling, allowing automated account creation and reset-token spam.]

Password reset tokens written to plaintext log file — Anyone with filesystem read access can obtain valid password reset tokens and take over any user account that requests a reset. [verified: The raw password-reset token is written to password_reset_mailbox.log at auth.py line 248 before hashing, with no access control on the log file; anyone with filesystem read access to the project directory can harvest active tokens and reset passwords.]

Password reset tokens and initial passwords written to plaintext log file — An attacker with local filesystem read access to the backend directory can harvest plaintext password reset tokens and initial passwords, enabling account takeover of any user whose token appears in the log. [verified: Same pattern as finding 0 but across four endpoints (auth.py:248, users.py:79/147, imports_exports.py:318): plaintext initial passwords and reset tokens are appended to password_reset_mailbox.log with no encryption or access restriction, exposing credentials to anyone with filesystem read access.]

CSV export authorization bypass — underwriters can export all applications including drafts — Underwriters can bulk-export sensitive data for all applications including drafts they are not authorized to view, exposing business names, loan purposes, amounts, and confirming the existence of confidential draft applications [verified: The export_applications_csv endpoint at imports_exports.py:66-68 checks `actor.role in (admin, underwriter)` but applies NO data-scope filter for underwriters, while list_applications at applications.py:129-141 restricts underwriters to `assigned_underwriter_id == actor.id OR status in [submitted, in_review, needs_documents, counteroffered]` — allowing any underwriter to bulk-export all applicatio]

Initial passwords written to plaintext log during CSV lead import — Anyone with filesystem or log aggregation access can obtain valid initial passwords for imported borrower accounts, enabling unauthorized access. [verified: Line 319 writes the plaintext initial password (secrets.token_urlsafe(16)) to password_reset_mailbox.log on a reachable admin endpoint (POST /imports/borrower-leads). No encryption or access control protects the log file; the same insecure pattern exists at users.py:74 (user creation) and auth.py:~248 (reset tokens). The threat model lists this pattern as a known concern.]

Initial and temporary passwords written to plaintext log file — Anyone with filesystem read access can obtain valid credentials for newly created users and admin-reset accounts, enabling account takeover. [verified: Initial/temporary plaintext passwords are written to password_reset_mailbox.log at three code sites (users.py:79, users.py:147, imports_exports.py:318) with only .gitignore as a file-exclusion measure — no encryption, access restriction, or secure delivery channel exists; anyone with local filesystem read access can harvest valid credentials for newly created, admin-reset, or CSV-imported accounts]

Account enumeration via distinct lockout HTTP response — An attacker can enumerate which email addresses have accounts in the system by triggering lockouts (e.g., submitting 8 bad passwords for each candidate email), then observing the 429 response. This enables targeted credential stuffing, spear-phishing, or social engineering attacks against confirmed account holders. [verified: After 8 failed logins a real account returns HTTP 429 ('Account temporarily locked') while a non-existent account returns HTTP 401 ('Invalid email or password'); this creates an enumeration oracle, though exploitation requires 8 requests per candidate and is gated by a 15-minute lockout window.]
